subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 4 periods = 160 minutes
Total: 4 periods · 2h 40min

tasks_in_class.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.
Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____
How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines
Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour.

periods.activity_title: Spotting and naming shapes hidden in rangoli
materials: Pre-cut shape cut-outs (circles, squares, triangles, rectangles)
Large rangoli image or drawing on the board

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays a large rangoli image and invites children to call out shapes they recognise. Students then attempt Let us Do Q1, p.44 ("Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.") on their dot grids, working individually with pencils.

Students share their completed dot-grid rangoli with a partner, then complete Let us Do Q2, p.45 ("Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli....") by writing shape names. Class discussion follows: teacher draws out names — circle, square, triangle, rectangle — and accepts children's own words before settling on shared vocabulary.

Students tackle Let us Do Q3, p.45 ("How many shapes are made with curved lines / straight lines...."), sorting shapes into the two groups individually, then comparing counts in pairs. Teacher uses the sorting exercise to reinforce the curved/straight distinction.

Each student receives pre-cut shape cut-outs and creates their own rangoli design following Let us Do Q4, p.45 ("Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design...."). Students outline, colour, and caption their design with the shape names they used. Work is displayed or kept in notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is children calling any four-sided figure a square — during Q2 and Q3 prompt them to check whether all sides look the same or only opposite sides match. Shape cut-outs and the dot grid are the primary materials for this unit; have extras ready so every child can make a personal design. Naming shapes in the rangoli context anchors abstract vocabulary to a culturally familiar image that children can return to throughout the chapter.

homework.description: Try to make the following objects using shape cutouts.

tasks_in_class.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?
Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.
Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.

periods.activity_title: Unfolding boxes to find hidden flat faces
materials: Cardboard boxes of various sizes (one per group)
Small cuboidal objects — sharpeners, erasers, matchboxes (one per student)

time_bands.activity: Groups of three receive a cardboard box each and carefully open it flat, following Let us Do Q1, p.46 ("Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully...."). Groups examine the unfolded box and identify and name the shapes of the faces. Teacher circulates, asking: 'What shape is this face? Is it the same size as that face?'

Each child picks up a small cuboidal object — sharpener or eraser — and traces every face onto paper, then answers questions (a)–(f) from Let us Do Q1, p.48 ("Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object....") about the number of faces, their shapes, and whether any squares or triangles appear. Teacher prompts: 'Are all the rectangles you traced the same size?'

Class discussion on Let us Do p.47 ("Name any three objects that have rectangular faces...."). Students share their lists aloud and the teacher builds a class list on the board, drawing out the observation that many everyday objects — books, boxes, doors — are cuboid in form and that all their faces are rectangles or squares.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often expect all faces of a box to be identical rectangles; the tracing task (Q1, p.48) is designed to surface the surprise that different faces can be different-sized rectangles. The envelope-making activity (Let us Do Q2, p.46) can serve as an extension for early finishers — fold a square sheet as shown to discover what shapes emerge. Encourage children to name the specific 2D shapes they find rather than using vague words like 'flat'.

tasks_in_class.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.
Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.
Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

periods.activity_title: Building and describing rectangles on dot grids
materials: Board or chart with sample differently-oriented rectangles

time_bands.activity: Students use dot grids to complete Let us Do Q2, p.49 ("Construct the rectangles using the sides given below."), joining given pairs of dots to form rectangles of different lengths and widths. Teacher invites children to say how they know their shape is a rectangle — laying the ground for a property conversation.

Students work on Let us Do Q3, p.49 ("Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle."), drawing three successively larger rectangles on their dot grid that all share the same centre. Teacher points out that each new rectangle still has two long and two short sides.

Class examines the differently-oriented rectangles in Let us Do Q5, p.50 ("Look at the different rectangles....") and answers all four parts — sides, corners, equal sides, own description. Students share their own-words descriptions; teacher collects recurring vocabulary and writes it on the board, arriving together at: 4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is children assuming a rectangle must be wider than it is tall; presenting upright and tilted rectangles in Q5 directly challenges this. Additional practice: Let us Do Q4, p.50 (counting embedded rectangles) is assigned as homework and reinforces the property understanding built in class. Having children articulate properties in their own words before the teacher formalises them is key to this unit.

homework.description: Count and write the number of rectangles in the following picture.

section_titles: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles

tasks_in_class.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.
Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?
Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.
Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

periods.activity_title: Discovering what makes a square special
materials: Chess or ludo board tile (teacher demonstration)

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a chess board tile and a ludo board; students count squares visible. Children then complete Let us Do p.51 ("How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners."), filling blanks and discussing: 'Is a square like a rectangle? How?'

Students use matchsticks at their desks to attempt Let us Do Q2, p.52 ("Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides...."). Groups count and record how many small squares appear. Teacher gathers counts and asks: 'Why do all four sides of your matchstick shape look equal?'

Using square cut-outs, students explore Let us Do Q4, p.53 ("How many different shapes can you make by joining 2 squares / 3 squares / 4 squares....") and sketch each unique arrangement on a dot grid. Teacher circulates to check children are not repeating mirror images as new shapes.

Students complete Let us Explore Q1, p.53 ("Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why."), then share reasoning aloud. Teacher uses the discussion to consolidate: a square is always a rectangle, but a rectangle is not always a square.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error here is children insisting a square cannot be a rectangle because 'all sides are equal'; Q1 in Let us Explore directly addresses this and should not be rushed. Additional practice: Let us Do Q3, p.52 (completing squares from given sides) and Let us Explore Q2–Q3, p.53 (folding corners, triangle-cutting) may be used as extension activities. Having children physically stack a square cut-out on a rectangle cut-out helps them see the shared corner property.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw a simple rangoli design that uses at least one circle, one triangle, and one rectangle. Label each shape you have used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A design containing at least one circle, one triangle, and one rectangle, each labelled correctly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify shapes by their appearance — curved boundary for circle, three sides for triangle, four sides with opposite sides equal for rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide pre-drawn shapes to trace; stretch: add a fourth shape type and count how many of each appear.

exercise.description: Make Amma's rangoli on the dots given below.

items.prompt: Choose two shapes from your rangoli. Draw each shape in the box below and write whether its boundary is made of curved lines, straight lines, or both.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Circle — curved line; triangle or rectangle — straight lines; any shape using both correctly identified.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trace the boundary of the shape mentally: a circle has only a curved edge, while triangles and rectangles have only straight edges.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student run a finger along the edge of a cut-out; stretch: find a shape in the room that uses both curved and straight edges and sketch it.

exercise.description: Use cut outs of shapes to make a rangoli design. Outline the object and colour.

items.prompt: Take your geometry box or any rectangular box. Trace one face of the box on your notebook. Write the name of the shape you got and say whether all the sides you traced are equal or only the opposite sides are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A traced rectangle (or square if the face happens to be square); for a rectangle — opposite sides are equal; for a square — all sides are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The faces of a cuboid are rectangles or squares; check side equality by visual comparison of opposite pairs.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: trace two different faces and compare; stretch: trace all six faces and see how many different-sized rectangles appear.

exercise.description: Collect some cardboard boxes and open them up carefully. What shapes do you see in the flattened boxes?

items.prompt: Priya traced all the faces of her eraser onto paper. Which statement best describes what she found?

options.label: A
options.text: All faces were circles.

options.label: B
options.text: All faces were the same size rectangle.

options.label: C
options.text: Some faces were triangles and some were rectangles.

options.label: D
options.text: The faces were rectangles, but they could be different sizes.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The faces were rectangles, but they could be different sizes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A cuboid has six rectangular faces; opposite faces are identical, but the three pairs need not all be the same size.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not traced different faces — they assume all faces of a cuboid look the same.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused 3D objects with 2D shapes and does not yet know that cuboid faces cannot be triangles.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected 3D objects to 2D faces at all — likely a very early confusion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: physically open a small box and point to two clearly different-sized rectangular faces; stretch: predict which face will be largest before tracing.

exercise.description: Trace all the faces of any cuboidal object (example—sharpener or eraser). Answer (a)–(f) about faces, shapes, squares, and triangles.

items.prompt: On the dot grid below, draw a rectangle that is 4 dots wide and 2 dots tall. Then draw one more rectangle that is larger than the first one. Label each rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: First rectangle correctly joining dots 4 wide and 2 tall; second rectangle with at least one dimension larger, correctly closed, labelled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the dot grid to count dots for width and height, then join the four corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark the four corner dots before drawing; stretch: draw a third rectangle that is larger still and write the width and height of each.

exercise.description: Construct the rectangles using the sides given below.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Use matchsticks (or draw matchstick-sized lines) to make one square. Now add more matchsticks touching the sides of your first square to make more squares, so that every outer side of the arrangement is also a square. Draw what you made and write how many squares you can count.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A 2×2 arrangement of four small squares, giving 4 small squares plus 1 large square = 5 squares in total (or any other valid configuration correctly counted).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Build the arrangement by sharing sides, then count all squares including the large outer one.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start with real matchsticks before drawing; stretch: extend to a 3×3 arrangement and count all squares.

exercise.description: Use matchsticks to make a square so that it has squares on all its sides. How many squares did you get?

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Join 3 equal square units on your dot grid. Draw all the different shapes you can make. How many different shapes did you find? (Two shapes are the same if one can be slid to look exactly like the other.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two distinct triomino shapes: a straight row of 3 squares, and an L-shaped arrangement of 3 squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place three unit squares sharing full sides; slide arrangements to check for duplicates — only two distinct shapes exist.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: cut out three square pieces and move them physically; stretch: now try 4 squares and report the count.

exercise.description: Use the square cutouts: How many different shapes can you make by joining (a) 2 squares (b) 3 squares (c) 4 squares. Show them in a dot grid.

items.prompt: On your dot grid, connect dots to draw two different squares — one small and one large. Put a small square symbol (□) at every square corner of each shape you drew.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two correctly drawn squares of different sizes, each with a square-corner symbol at all four corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A square has four square corners; mark each with a small □ symbol at the corner point.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use the corner of a notebook to check each corner before marking; stretch: draw a rectangle alongside and explain why all four corners of a rectangle are also square corners.

exercise.description: Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?

items.prompt: Draw three objects from everyday life that have a triangular face. Write the name of each object beside its drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any three valid objects whose visible face is triangular, e.g. a slice of watermelon, a musical triangle, a samosa, a caution sign, a tent — each labelled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A triangular face has exactly three straight sides and three corners.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: look around the classroom for ideas before drawing; stretch: for each object say whether its triangle looks the same as or different from the others.

exercise.description: Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook.

items.section_title: Circus with circles — circle and centre
items.prompt: Trace a round object (bottle cap or bangle) twice on your notebook to make two circles — one small and one large. Fold each traced circle in half. Mark the point where the two fold lines cross. What do you notice about this point on both circles?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The crossing point is at the middle (centre) of the circle; the same central point is found on both circles regardless of size.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Every fold line through a circle passes through the centre; where two folds cross is the centre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fold a pre-drawn circle cut-out instead of tracing; stretch: make three folds and confirm all three cross at the same point.

exercise.description: Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.

items.prompt: In the box below, create a border design that uses both curved lines and straight lines. Use at least two different kinds of shapes in your design.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any border pattern that clearly contains both curved elements and straight-line elements, with at least two shape types visible.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Alternate or mix curved and straight segments to form a repeating border unit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start with a single repeating unit and copy it three times; stretch: add a colour code to show which part of the pattern is straight and which is curved.

exercise.description: Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.

items.prompt: Using tangram pieces (or by drawing on dot paper), make one shape that looks like an animal or object. Write the names of the tangram pieces you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any recognisable composite shape formed from named tangram pieces (e.g. two large triangles + one small square); the piece names written correctly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fit tangram pieces edge-to-edge; name each piece by its shape — large triangle, small triangle, square, parallelogram.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: reproduce one of the given outlines from the textbook rather than inventing a new one; stretch: record how many pieces were used and what percentage are triangles.

exercise.description: Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

items.prompt: Sana sees these shapes in a rangoli: a circle, two rectangles, and a triangle. She says all the shapes with straight sides have corners. Is she right?

options.label: A
options.text: No — a rectangle has straight sides but no corners.

options.label: B
options.text: No — only circles have corners.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — but only if the shape has more than four sides.

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — shapes with straight sides always have corners.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Yes, shapes with straight sides always have corners.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Straight-sided shapes are closed figures; wherever two straight sides meet, they form a corner.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused the presence of sides with corners — they may think sides and corners are independent features.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the property: circles have no corners and no straight sides.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student believes corners only appear beyond four sides, suggesting incomplete understanding of how sides and corners relate.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student trace around a rectangle and count each turn as a corner; stretch: ask what shape has the fewest corners possible and why.

exercise.description: Name the shapes drawn in Amma's rangoli: _____, _____, _____

items.prompt: Ravi says: 'I can find triangles on the face of my pencil box.' Do you agree? Write yes or no and give a reason.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: No — a pencil box is a cuboid; all its faces are rectangles (or squares). None of its faces are triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The faces of a cuboid are always rectangles or squares; triangles cannot appear as cuboid faces.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: invite the student to trace each face of a real pencil box; stretch: name one 3D object whose faces could include a triangle.

exercise.description: Name any three objects that have rectangular faces.

items.prompt: Meera draws four rectangles in different positions — one lying flat, one standing tall, one tilted. She says they all have the same number of sides. Which answer also correctly describes ALL four rectangles?

options.label: A
options.text: A rectangle can only have equal sides if it is tilted.

options.label: B
options.text: All four sides of each rectangle are equal.

options.label: C
options.text: Each rectangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.

options.label: D
options.text: Each rectangle has 4 corners and its opposite sides are equal.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Each rectangle has 4 corners and its opposite sides are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count sides and corners on any rectangle, then compare opposite side pairs to see that opposite sides match.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused rectangle with square — they think all four sides must be equal.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has a misconception that orientation affects the equality of sides.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused rectangle with triangle — likely a naming error rather than property confusion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a ruler to measure one pair of opposite sides on a drawn rectangle; stretch: draw a shape that has 4 sides but is NOT a rectangle and explain what makes it different.

exercise.description: Look at the different rectangles given below: (a) How many sides? (b) How many corners? (c) Equal sides? (d) Describe in your own words.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: A chess tile has all four sides equal and four square corners. A door mat has opposite sides equal but not all four sides equal, and four square corners. Which statement is true?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the tile and the door mat are squares.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither is a rectangle because their corners are square.

options.label: C
options.text: The tile is a square and also a rectangle; the door mat is a rectangle but not a square.

options.label: D
options.text: The tile is a square but not a rectangle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — The tile is a square and also a rectangle; the door mat is a rectangle but not a square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A square satisfies all rectangle properties (4 sides, 4 square corners, opposite sides equal) and additionally has all four sides equal; so every square is a rectangle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks equal opposite sides are enough for a square — they have not grasped the all-sides-equal requirement.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student believes a square and a rectangle are completely separate shapes — a very common error this section addresses.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks square corners disqualify a shape from being a rectangle — a reversal of the defining property.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: physically place a square cut-out on a rectangle cut-out and trace — it fits the corner test for both; stretch: draw a Venn diagram labelled 'squares' and 'rectangles' and place each shape correctly.

exercise.description: How many squares do you see in this drawing? Both have ___ sides. Both have ___ corners.

items.section_title: Same to Same — squares vs rectangles
items.prompt: Look at these four shapes: a square, a rectangle, a circle, and a shape with 5 sides. Tick which ones are rectangles and write one reason why the others are NOT rectangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Square — rectangle (all 4 sides, 4 corners, opposite sides equal, all sides equal); Rectangle — rectangle; Circle — not a rectangle (no straight sides, no corners); Five-sided shape — not a rectangle (5 sides not 4).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check: does the shape have exactly 4 straight sides, 4 corners, and opposite sides equal? If not, it is not a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a checklist (4 sides? 4 corners? opposite sides equal?) to apply to each shape; stretch: draw one more shape that is also a rectangle and one that is not.

exercise.description: Tick the shapes that are rectangles. Which figures are not rectangles? Explain why.

items.prompt: Arjun checks the corners of a square and the corners of a rectangle using a corner-tester made from paper strips. What will he find?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the square and the rectangle have square corners at every corner.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither has square corners — only a right-angle ruler has square corners.

options.label: C
options.text: The rectangle has more square corners than the square.

options.label: D
options.text: The square has square corners but the rectangle does not.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — Both the square and the rectangle have square corners at every corner.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the corner-tester at each angle of the square and rectangle — it fits exactly each time, confirming all corners are square corners.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student thinks only squares have square corners — they have not yet generalised the property to all rectangles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student thinks the property belongs to a measuring instrument rather than to the shape itself.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing the number of corners with the type — both shapes have exactly 4 corners, all square.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically use the notebook corner as a tester on a drawn rectangle; stretch: find one shape in the room that does NOT have a square corner and explain how you know.

exercise.description: Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same? Name objects in class that have only square corners.

items.prompt: Murugan used 10 matchsticks to make three squares that share sides. If he uses 12 matchsticks in the same way, how many squares can he make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 squares
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Arrange matchsticks in a 2×2 grid: 3 horizontal sticks in each of 2 rows = 6, 3 vertical sticks in each of 2 columns = 6, total 12 matchsticks forming 4 unit squares.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use real matchsticks to build the arrangement physically; stretch: predict how many matchsticks would make 5 squares in a row.

exercise.description: Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

items.prompt: Six dots are placed evenly on a circle. How many different triangles can be drawn by joining any three of these dots with straight lines?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20 triangles
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose any 3 dots from 6 — the number of ways is 6×5×4 ÷ (3×2×1) = 20; each set of 3 dots gives exactly one triangle since no three dots are in a straight line on the circle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a printed circle with 4 dots first and count systematically; stretch: if one more dot were added to make 7, predict how many triangles there would be.

exercise.description: How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?

items.prompt: You have one triangle made from 3 matchsticks. You want to turn it into two triangles by moving exactly two matchsticks (without removing any). Describe where you would move the two matchsticks.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Move two matchsticks to form a shared side inside the original triangle, creating two smaller triangles that together fill the original shape (e.g. pick up two outer sides and reposition them to divide the interior). Any valid verbal or drawn description accepted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Rearrange two matchsticks so that a new line appears inside the triangle, dividing it into two triangular regions.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use real matchsticks before describing; stretch: try to make three triangles by moving two matchsticks from a different starting arrangement.

exercise.description: Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.

items.prompt: Compare a square and a triangle. Write one way they are the SAME and one way they are DIFFERENT.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Same — both have straight sides (or: both have corners); Different — a square has 4 sides and 4 corners, while a triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners (or: a square has all square corners, a triangle does not necessarily).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare number of sides and corners, type of corners, and nature of boundary.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw both shapes side by side and point to the features you are comparing; stretch: write a second similarity and a second difference.

exercise.description: Look at these two shapes (square and triangle): discuss similarities and differences. Tick (a) corners: same/different (b) number of sides: same/different.

items.prompt: In a triangle-row picture: the first figure has 1 triangle, the second figure (two rows) has 4 triangles. How many triangles will the third figure (three rows) have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 triangles
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Row 1 adds 1 triangle; row 2 adds 3 more (total 4); row 3 adds 5 more (total 9) — the count grows by consecutive odd numbers, giving n² for n rows.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the first two figures and count aloud to find the pattern; stretch: predict the count for 4 rows and explain the pattern in your own words.

exercise.description: I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure? If one more row, how many in the third figure?

items.prompt: Here are three shapes: a circle, a square, and a triangle. Your friend says the circle is the odd one out. Give one reason your friend could be right AND one reason the triangle could also be the odd one out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Circle as odd one out: it has no straight sides and no corners, while the other two do. Triangle as odd one out: it has 3 sides and 3 corners, while the other two have 4 sides and 4 corners (square) or are circular.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare one attribute at a time — type of boundary, number of sides, number of corners — and use whichever attribute isolates the chosen shape.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list two features of each shape first; stretch: can the square also be the odd one out? Find a reason.

exercise.description: Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd? Discuss.

items.prompt: A rangoli has 3 circles, 2 triangles, and 4 rectangles. How many of these shapes are made with curved lines only?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Circles have curved boundaries only; there are 3 circles, so the answer is 3.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counted triangles instead of circles — may be confusing shape names with counts.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added triangles and circles (2 + 3 = 5) or some other incorrect combination.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added all shapes (3 + 2 + 4 = 9) without filtering for curved-line shapes.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a small circle, triangle, and rectangle and label which type of line each uses; stretch: write how many shapes are made with straight lines only.

exercise.description: How many shapes are made with (a) Curved lines (b) Straight lines

items.prompt: A rectangle is already drawn on your dot grid. Draw two more rectangles, each larger than the previous one, around it so that all three share the same centre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two correctly drawn rectangles, each visibly larger than the inner one, all aligned on the dot grid with consistent proportions.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Extend each side of the inner rectangle by the same number of dot-spaces outward on all four sides to keep the shapes centred.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark the centre point first and extend equally from it; stretch: write the width and height of each rectangle to show they increase by the same step.

exercise.description: Draw 3 bigger rectangles around the given rectangle.

items.prompt: Nita draws a shape with 4 sides and marks all its corners. She tests each corner with a paper-strip tester. Two corners fit the tester exactly, and two corners are wider. How many square corners does Nita's shape have?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: A corner is a square corner only when the paper-strip tester fits exactly — two corners fit, so the answer is 2.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student did not register the two corners that fit — possibly confused 'fits exactly' with 'does not fit'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student thinks a 4-sided shape must have 4 square corners — confusing it with a rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has miscounted — perhaps adding the 2 fitting + 1 extra from the wider corners incorrectly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the shape and mark each corner as 'square' or 'wider' using symbols; stretch: sketch what Nita's shape might look like.

exercise.description: Mark the square corners in these shapes.

items.prompt: In your notebook, draw a triangle in three different sizes. Then draw a rectangle in two different orientations — one lying flat and one standing tall. Label each drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Three triangles of visibly different sizes, all correctly closed with three sides and three corners; two rectangles — one wide, one tall — each correctly closed with four sides and four square corners; all labelled.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Vary the length of two sides to change the size of a triangle; rotate the same pair of dimensions to change the orientation of a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use dot paper to help control the size and orientation; stretch: add a circle in two different sizes beside the triangles and rectangles.

exercise.description: Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.

items.prompt: A rectangle has a gap shaped like a right-angled triangle cut from one corner. Which piece would fill the gap to make the rectangle complete again?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle piece of the same size.

options.label: B
options.text: A rectangle piece the same size as the original.

options.label: C
options.text: A right-angled triangle piece that fits the corner exactly.

options.label: D
options.text: A square piece twice the size of the gap.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — A right-angled triangle piece that fits the corner exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the shape and size of the gap — it is a right-angled triangle, so only a congruent right-angled triangle piece fills it.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is not attending to the shape of the gap — a curved piece cannot fill a triangular corner.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is thinking of the piece as larger than needed — they may not be visualising the fit.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing the gap with the whole rectangle — they have not isolated the missing piece.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: cut out the gap shape from paper and physically try placing it; stretch: describe what two pieces together could also fill the gap.

exercise.description: To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps in the shape on the right side.

items.prompt: A house shape is made from a rectangle with a triangle on top. Draw two straight lines inside this shape to split it into exactly three triangles. Show your lines on the drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two lines drawn inside the house shape that divide it into three non-overlapping triangular regions. One valid solution: one diagonal across the rectangular base creates two triangles from the base; the triangular roof remains the third triangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Draw one diagonal in the rectangular base to make two triangles; the roof triangle is the third.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: cut out the house shape and fold it once to visualise where a line might go; stretch: find a second way to draw two different lines that also create three triangles.

exercise.description: Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.

items.prompt: An L-shaped figure is given. Draw exactly one straight line inside it to split it into three triangles. Show your line on the drawing.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One straight line drawn inside the L-shape from one vertex to another non-adjacent vertex, splitting the L into three triangular regions. One valid solution: draw a diagonal from the inner re-entrant corner to a far outer corner, producing three triangles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the re-entrant corner of the L and draw one line to a far corner; this cuts the L into three triangular parts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: trace the outline of the L on paper, cut it out, and try folding once to see where a line might go; stretch: verify your answer by counting the triangles and checking each region has exactly three sides.

exercise.description: Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.

Mark the square corners in these shapes.
Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?
Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?

dropped_units.activity_title: Testing and making square corners everywhere
materials: Two short paper strips per student joined with a split pin (angle-tester)

time_bands.activity: Each student receives two short paper strips joined with a split pin to form a pivoting angle-tester. They open the strips to different angles and compare each against the corner of their notebook, deciding whether their angle is less than, equal to, or more than a square corner. Discussion follows from Let us Do p.54 ("Are the corners of a square the same? Are corners of square and rectangle the same?...") as children test real classroom objects.

Students use their angle-testers on the printed shapes in Let us Do Q1, p.55 ("Mark the square corners in these shapes.") to identify and mark square corners with a small square symbol. Teacher draws attention to shapes that have some but not all square corners.

Students work on Let us Do Q2, p.55 ("Connect the dots to make some squares. How many different squares did you get?") on a dot grid, joining dots in different ways to form squares of varied sizes. Teacher invites children to share their count and ask: 'Did anyone find a large square that contains a smaller one?'

Students take matchsticks and attempt Let us Do Q5, p.56 ("Murugan made three squares with 10 matchsticks. How many squares can you make with 12 matchsticks?"). Groups discuss sharing of sides; teacher uses the puzzle to deepen reasoning about how squares connect and how square corners are preserved in arrangements.

dropped_units.teacher_notes: The angle-tester made from paper strips lets children feel the difference between a sharp corner, a square corner, and an obtuse corner before they mark them on paper — moving from concrete to pictorial is crucial here. A common error is marking every corner of a triangle as a square corner; using the tester physically on the triangle's corners reveals the mismatch. Additional practice: Let us Do Q4, p.56 (drawing two-matchstick and four-matchstick square-corner arrangements) can be offered as extension.

homework.description: Look at the picture: (a) Count and write the number of corners. (b) Circle the square corners.

section_titles: Circus with circles — circle and centre

tasks_in_class.description: Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself, in your notebook.
How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?
Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.
Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings in your notebook.
Try to make a circle on the playground.

dropped_units.activity_title: Three corners, no corners — triangles and circles together
materials: Pre-printed dot-circle sheet for Q3, p.57
Bottle caps, bangles, or circular rings (a few per group)
Paper plates (one per student or per group)
Chalk and a length of rope (for playground circle)

time_bands.activity: Students open their notebooks and complete Let us Do Q1, p.57 ("Draw and name some triangular objects that you see around yourself...."), drawing at least three triangular objects from their environment. Pairs share; teacher compiles a quick class list on the board and asks: 'What do all these shapes have in common?'

Students investigate Let us Do Q3, p.57 ("How many different triangles can be made using the dots on this circle?"), working with a pre-printed circle with dots. Teacher encourages systematic listing and asks: 'Have you found all of them? How do you know?' Students then attempt Let us Do Q4, p.57 ("Move two matchsticks to turn the one triangle into two triangles.") with real matchsticks, reasoning about which two sticks to move.

Transition to circles: students use bottle caps, bangles, and rings to trace circles in their notebooks, following Let us Do Q3, p.58 ("Draw circles by tracing bottle caps, bangles, and rings...."). Teacher holds up traced circles of different sizes and asks: 'What is the same about all of them? Do circles have corners? Sides?'

If space allows, students head to a courtyard or open area and attempt Let us Do p.59 ("Try to make a circle on the playground.") using a rope or chalk. Back in class (or in the same space), the teacher demonstrates folding a paper plate in half, then in half again, marking where folds meet, establishing intuitively that all folds pass through one central point.

dropped_units.teacher_notes: Children sometimes count a triangle twice if its orientation is different — the dot-circle task (Q3, p.57) is a good place to surface and correct this by having them label each triangle they find. When moving from triangles to circles, the contrast 'three corners / no corners' is worth naming explicitly to reinforce both. The paper-plate folding demonstration is the key concrete experience for the circle-centre idea; have a pre-folded plate ready to show the centre quickly if playground time is short.

dropped_units.activity_title: Comparing, splitting, and building shapes — part one
materials: Shape cut-outs (optional, for Q2 pair comparison)

time_bands.activity: Students complete Let us Do Q1, p.60 ("Look at these two shapes...."), ticking same/different for corners and number of sides, then discuss in pairs. They move to Let us Do Q2, p.60 ("Choose any pair of shapes...."), picking their own pair and articulating at least two similarities and two differences aloud to their partner; selected pairs share with the class.

Students study the growing triangle-row figure in Let us Do Q4, p.61 ("I made one triangle, then another row. How many triangles in second figure?..."), counting carefully and predicting the count for a third row. Teacher invites two or three students to explain their reasoning strategy — counting row by row versus finding a pattern.

Class discussion around Let us Do Q6, p.62 ("Each of these shapes can be the odd one out. How is each one odd?..."). Teacher presents one shape at a time and students justify in their own words; multiple valid justifications are accepted and celebrated. The task builds the habit of reading shape attributes flexibly.

Students independently work through Let us Do Q7, p.62 ("To complete the rectangle, tick the appropriate shapes from the left side to fill the gaps...."), visualising which pieces fill which gap. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'What shape is the gap? Which piece from the left matches that shape?'

dropped_units.teacher_notes: The odd-one-out discussion (Q6, p.62) often surprises children because there is no single right answer — affirm all well-reasoned responses to build mathematical confidence. The triangle-row growth task (Q4, p.61) is the chapter's main pattern task; children who count all triangles individually rather than looking for a pattern can be gently nudged with 'Is there a quick way to see how many are added each time?' Additional practice: Let us Do Q3, p.61 (finding the largest rectangle) and Q5, p.61 (counting torn square pieces) may be noted for early finishers.

tasks_in_class.description: Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.
Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles.
Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations in your notebook: (a) Triangle (b) Rectangle (c) Circle (d) Any other shape of your choice.
Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.
Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle given in the end of the book. Can you create these shapes using some of the pieces?

dropped_units.activity_title: Splitting shapes, drawing freely, and creating patterns
materials: Tangram pieces cut from the back of the textbook (one set per student)
Scissors (if tangram pieces need cutting in class)

time_bands.activity: Students draw two lines inside the printed house-shaped figure from Let us Do Q8, p.62 ("Draw two lines to split the shape into three triangles.") and one line inside the L-shaped figure from Let us Do Q9, p.62 ("Draw one line to split the shape into 3 triangles."). Teacher circulates offering only spatial prompts: 'Where could your first line start?' Students compare solutions with neighbours.

Students open their notebooks and complete Let us Do Q10, p.62 ("Make the following shapes with different sizes and orientations...."), drawing each of the four shapes — triangle, rectangle, circle, and a free choice — at least twice, in different sizes and orientations. Teacher highlights examples where a rectangle is drawn tall rather than wide, reinforcing that orientation does not change the shape's identity.

Students turn to Doors-dots-lines p.63 ("Try to make your own border designs using both curved and straight lines.") and create a personal border design, deliberately combining curved and straight lines. Teacher invites a few children to show their design and name the shapes or types of lines they used.

Students use the tangram pieces cut from the back of their book to attempt Tangram p.63 ("Use the pieces from the tangram puzzle...."), building the given outline shapes. Teacher encourages trial and rotation of pieces, asking: 'Which piece might fit this corner? Can you turn it?' The unit closes with children sharing which tangram shape they found most satisfying to make.

dropped_units.teacher_notes: The two splitting tasks (Q8 and Q9, p.62) are the chapter's main spatial puzzle challenges; children who are stuck can be offered a cut-out of the shape so they can draw a fold line physically before committing to paper. A common difficulty with the tangram is children placing pieces in the original orientation only — prompt them to try rotating and flipping. The border-design activity and the tangram together consolidate the full vocabulary of shapes — straight, curved, triangle, rectangle, square, circle — that has been built across the chapter.
